title: How do energy companies and utilities make money, and what matters in their cases?
description: Energy and utilities economics for case interviews: regulated returns, generation costs, capacity, the energy transition and rooftop solar, with a worked…
hook: Energy cases are increasingly common because the energy transition is reshaping the industry. Utilities are often regulated, investments are huge and long-lived, and new technologies like solar and batteries are changing who makes money.
body:
The main businesses

  • Generation: making electricity from gas, wind, solar, nuclear and more.
  • Networks: the grid that moves power, often regulated monopolies earning an allowed return.
  • Retail: selling energy to homes and businesses, a competitive, thin-margin business.

Long-lived investments

Power plants and grids last decades, so payback and NPV matter a lot in these cases.

A worked example: rooftop solar's effect on a utility

A utility sells 10,000 GWh a year to homes. If 10% of homes install solar and cut their grid use by 40%, sales fall by 10% × 40% = 4%, or 400 GWh. But the grid's costs are mostly fixed, so the same costs are spread over fewer units, pushing prices up for everyone else and encouraging even more solar.

Typical energy case questions

  • How should a utility respond to rooftop solar?
  • Should we invest in a wind farm or battery storage?
  • Should a city or government back a new nuclear plant?
  • How should an oil company plan for falling demand?

Separate generation, grids and retail before proposing a solution

An energy company can generate electricity, operate regulated network assets, sell power to customers or combine these activities. They earn money differently. A generator's economics depend on production, realised prices, fuel or operating costs and capital intensity. A regulated grid's economics often depend on an allowed return on invested assets plus performance incentives. Retail suppliers face customer churn, acquisition costs and the risk of buying energy at prices above what their contracts recover.

Consider a wind farm with 100 MW of installed capacity, a 35% capacity factor and an illustrative realised price of £65 per MWh. Annual electricity produced is 100 × 8,760 × 35% = 306,600 MWh, producing around £19.9 million gross revenue before operating costs, curtailment and financing. Changing the capacity factor from 35% to 30% cuts annual revenue by about £2.85 million at the same price. This example shows why a nameplate capacity number is not the same as annual output.

For a rooftop-solar case, first identify who is affected. A household may buy fewer units of grid electricity while still depending on the grid at night. A network operator may still incur fixed costs to serve that household. A retailer may lose sales volume, but gain opportunities in installation, batteries or flexibility services. The effects cannot be combined into one simplistic statement that solar is 'good' or 'bad' for utilities.

Ask which part of the value chain the client owns, which charges are regulated, and what risks come from wholesale prices, weather and policy. Recommendations in this sector should identify investment horizon and cash requirements.
